big_idea: Every pattern has a core — the part that repeats.
learning_intention: We are learning to find the core of a repeating pattern and explain why the core matters.
student_learning_goal: I can find the part of the pattern that repeats. We call it the core.
success_criteria: I can point to the core of a pattern.
I can use the loop frame to mark the core.
I can tell a friend why the core is important.
lesson_specific_materials: Drum or shaker (recommended for this lesson)
Anchor chart from Lesson 1 — add the word CORE today
Pre-built parade strips with 4 different patterns laid out (teacher prep, ~5 min)
Class formative tracker (provided in assessment_suite stage)

minds_on.hook: Coco's parade has a beat — and once you hear the beat, the parade can go on forever.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Gather children on the carpet. Hold up the Coco puppet and the drum.

Say to students: 'Coco brought a drum today. Listen closely — Coco is going to play the beat of the parade.' Tap the drum while saying animal names: 'Bea — Finn — Bea — Finn — Bea — Finn.' Stop. 'Did you hear something that kept coming back?' Take 2–3 responses. Confirm: 'Yes — Bea-Finn, Bea-Finn, Bea-Finn. That little part that keeps coming back is called the CORE of the pattern.'

Write CORE on the anchor chart underneath PATTERN. Draw a small loop around an imaginary pair to represent the idea visually. 'The core is the smallest part of the pattern that keeps repeating. Today we are going to be Core Detectives.'
student_actions: Listen quietly while the teacher drums and chants.
Identify aloud what they heard repeating.
Repeat the word 'core' as a class.

steps.instruction: Whole group: lay a Parade Strip (M2) flat. Place Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn on the six cells. Pick up a Core Loop Frame (M5) and place it around just the first Bea and Finn.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Watch what I do with the loop.' Place the loop around the first Bea-Finn pair. 'I lassoed the core. Bea-Finn is the smallest part that keeps repeating. After Bea-Finn comes Bea-Finn, and after that — Bea-Finn again.'

steps.instruction: Show an ABC pattern: Bea-Finn-Bibi-Bea-Finn-Bibi. Invite a child to come up and place the loop on the core.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now Coco's parade is bigger. Who can come up and lasso the core?' (After placement.) 'How did you know to put the loop around three cells and not two? Tell us what you noticed.'

steps.instruction: Trick example: lay out a strip with random animals (no repeating order). Ask the class to find the core.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Hmm — where is the core in this one?' Pause for confusion. 'Wait — is there a core? Why not?' Lead to: 'There is no core because nothing is repeating. Without a core, it is not a pattern, just a line of animals.'

steps.instruction: Send children to partner spots. Each pair gets 4 pre-built parade strips and one Core Loop Frame. Their job: place the loop on the core of each strip. Then: build one new parade together and loop its core.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are Core Detectives. You have four parades to solve. Place the loop around the core of each one. When you finish all four, build your own parade and loop your own core. Whisper your core to your partner before you make your loop.'

steps.instruction: Circulate. Use the formative tracker to record which children can identify, loop, and explain the core.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask: 'Where is the core in this parade? How do you know?' Record on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Use only AB strips for these children. Pre-mark the loop position with a faint pencil outline so they can place the loop on top.
differentiation.for_extending: Hand the pair a strip where the same core appears in two different colourings (e.g., one strip Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn, another Bibi-Moss-Bibi-Moss). Ask: 'Are the cores the same or different? Why?' (Foreshadows Lesson 3.)
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pair physical demonstration with each prompt. Allow the child to nod or place the loop without speaking. Use the words 'this part' and gesture if 'core' is not yet anchored.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After looping the strip, the pair walks the parade. Each time they reach the start of a new core, they say 'CORE!' aloud.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child place the loop on the correct cells? Can they explain that the core is what repeats, in their own words? Do they recognize when there is no core?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the formative tracker for each child as you circulate.
tracker_columns: Explains why it is the core

discussion_prompts: Why do we look for the core of a pattern?
If you know the core, what can you do next?
What's the difference between a parade with a core and just a line of animals?
consolidation.exit_routine: Quick 'core or no core' sort: teacher claps three short sequences (one with a core, one without, one with). Children show thumbs up for core, thumbs down for no core. Then each child taps the core on a classmate's parade strip before tidying.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class formative tracker for A7.2, plus completed student worksheet 'Find the Beat'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A7.2 is the keystone expectation of the unit. The teacher needs to know which children have internalized 'the core is what repeats' before Lesson 3 asks them to translate one core into multiple representations.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Lasso the Core — finding what repeats versus what's there
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: Step 3's 'trick example' (a strip of random animals) is the moment that exposes whether children have generalised 'core = the repeating part' or memorised 'core = some animals.' Step 4's partner work then makes them apply the loop independently. This is the conceptual centre of the unit — every later lesson assumes children own the word 'core.'
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Six pre-built parade strips ready at the carpet. Three have clear AB cores (Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn), two have ABC cores (Bea-Finn-Bibi repeated), and one is a 'trick' — six different animals in random order with NO repeating unit. One Core Loop Frame (M5) sits centred on the carpet. Children sit in a U around the strips.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Pick up the trick strip — Bea, Moss, Finn, Bibi, Bea, Moss. Hold it up. 'Friends, look at this parade. Where does the core go?' Watch hands shoot up. Call on a confident child. If they place the loop around the first two animals (Bea-Moss), look puzzled. 'Hmm. If Bea-Moss is the core, that means it should come back. Let me check…' Slide your finger from the loop along the strip. 'After Bea-Moss I see Finn. Not Bea-Moss again. So is Bea-Moss really the core?' Wait. Some children will say 'no!' Others will be unsure. Try another child's guess. Each time, slide your finger to test. Eventually the class will realise: 'There IS no core!'

This is the magical moment. 'Friends — sometimes a line of animals is just a line. It's NOT a pattern. A pattern needs a core. The core has to come BACK.' Pause. Hold up a clear AB strip alongside. 'This one IS a pattern. This one is NOT. What's the difference?' Take responses. Listen for 'it repeats' or 'it comes back.' If a child says 'this one has a beat,' celebrate it — that's the language from Coco's Drum Discovery and is exactly the conceptual hook you want to build on.

Send pairs to their work. Walk the room. The tell is the loop placement: tight loop on the first repeating unit means understanding. Loose loop spanning the whole strip means the child thinks 'the whole thing is the core.' Step in immediately.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Places loop around any two adjacent animals. Hasn't tested for repetition.
(Mid) Places loop correctly on AB but is unsure about ABC. Needs to see the third element 'come back.'
(Strong) Says 'there is no core' on the trick strip — full conceptual ownership.
(Strong) After looping AB on their own strip, draws a finger circle and says 'and again, and again, and again' — extends the core mentally.
common_misconceptions: The core is the whole pattern. (Child loops the entire strip rather than just the repeating unit.)
Any two adjacent animals form the core. (Child applies 'first two' rule mechanically without testing for repeat.)
Every line of animals has a core. (Child has not yet seen that some sequences are NOT patterns at all.)
recovery_moves: Test the loop with the finger-slide. Place the loop where the child put it, then slide your finger forward and ask 'does this come back?' Make the test visible.

Use the trick strip again 1:1. Privately, hand the child the random strip and ask 'where would the loop go?' When they struggle, say 'there is NO core. This isn't a pattern.' That single counter-example unlocks the concept faster than ten correct examples.
Anchor to the body. Have the child clap an AB they can hear (clap-stomp-clap-stomp). Ask 'what's the part that came back?' Then map the body answer onto the strip.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A7.2 — identifying and marking the core, and recognizing when a sequence is or is not a pattern.

parts_outline.task: Three short parade strips, each showing a repeating pattern (one AB, one ABC, one ABB). Student draws a loop or circle around the core of each.
A parade strip with the core already boxed at the start. Student extends the pattern by drawing or stickering three more cells.
Empty parade strip. Student creates their own pattern using two or three animals AND draws a loop around their core.
